Definition: Whether government taxes, customs duties, and other revenue can be paid using the instant digital payment system, indicating integration of payment infrastructure with tax administration systems.
Comments: Revenue collection via digital channels is active: URA provides tax payment services through MTN MoMo (enabling seamless digital payments and improving collections/compliance), demonstrating digital revenue collection.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed via URA's own e-services (Make a Payment/PRN generation, e-filing) and the December 2025 URA-MTN MoMo enhanced tax payment launch; multiple tax types (income, VAT, NTR fees) are payable digitally, supporting Value Code 3 (Yes).

Definition: Whether the instant payment system enables or plans to enable instant payments across national borders to other countries or regional payment systems, supporting remittances, trade, and regional integration.
Comments: Cross-border functionality exists via regional infrastructure such as the East African Payment System (EAPS), with BoU reporting EAPS inflows (UGX 1.3 trillion, +17% in FY2024/25), suggesting partially functional regional cross-border payments (not continent-wide instant).
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed: BoU's RTGS already supports the East African Payment System (EAPS) and COMESA's REPSS, and Uganda is now listed as a live PAPSS participant (June 2026 network coverage list). However, settlement still partly runs via USD/EUR conversion and onboarding of Ugandan banks to PAPSS is ongoing, so 'Partially functional' (Value Code 4) remains the better fit rather than 'Fully functional'.

Comments: The National Payment Systems Act explicitly classifies RTGS and ACH as “payment systems operated by the central bank” and assigns BoU functions to “regulate, supervise and oversee” payment systems, showing direct operation of core payment systems (RTGS/ACH).

Definition: Whether consumer protection legislation or regulations specifically address digital payment services, covering disclosure requirements, liability allocation for unauthorized transactions, error resolution procedures, and user rights.
Comments: The National Payment Systems Act includes consumer protection requirements for payment service providers and empowers BoU to prescribe consumer protection standards (e.g., principles include transparency, accountability, confidentiality, and dispute resolution).

revision_notes: Stronger evidence found: the National Payment Systems (Consumer Protection) Regulations, 2022 establish a dedicated complaints-handling and redress framework, disclosure requirements and consumer-asset protection, confirming Value Code 3 (Yes) with a more authoritative source than the Act's general provisions alone.

Definition: Whether legal or regulatory requirements obligate payment service providers to notify users, regulators, and/or data protection authorities about payment data breaches, cybersecurity incidents, or unauthorized access within specified timeframes.
Comments: Uganda’s Data Protection and Privacy Act/Regulations require breach notification: Section 23 of the Act and Regulation 33 impose a duty to notify the Personal Data Protection Office when there is reasonable belief personal data was accessed/acquired by an unauthorized person (PDPO then determines data-subject notification).
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed with the primary regulation text: Section 23 of the Data Protection and Privacy Act and Regulation 33 of the 2021 Regulations require immediate notification of the Personal Data Protection Office of a suspected breach, matching Value Code 3 (Mandatory).

Definition: Whether payment system governance explicitly includes mechanisms to ensure inclusivity and represent interests of vulnerable populations, including provisions for input from all participant types, consumer representatives, small providers, or explicit financial inclusion mandates in governance documents.
Comments: Uganda’s National Financial Inclusion Strategy II (2023–2028) includes governance mechanisms (e.g., Steering Committee and working groups) focused on reducing exclusion/access barriers and deepening use of quality financial services, indicating pro-inclusion governance with explicit poverty reduction/underserved group focus but not specific to a single payment scheme rulebook.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed: NFIS II (2023-2028) has a governance structure (Steering Committee, Inter-Institutional Committee, working groups) and explicit sections on underserved segments (women, youth, elderly, refugees, PWDs), but no scheme-specific consumer/PSP board representation was found — supports 'Partial' (Value Code 2) rather than a full Yes.

Definition: Whether the scheme rules governing payment system participation, pricing structure, technical requirements, security standards, and conduct are publicly accessible via website, public repository, or on request. Transparency indicator.
Comments: The National Payment Systems Act requires payment system operators to develop payment system rules “with the approval of the central bank,” but does not establish that scheme rulebooks are publicly published; no official public rulebook for a national instant payment scheme (e.g., National Payment Switch) was found in sources searched.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Revised upward: Section 11(6) of the NPS Act legally requires operators to publish payment system rules on their website within 14 days of BoU approval, and BoU's own site publicly lists its legal/regulatory framework and the Schedules to the UNISS Rules and Procedures. This is stronger than 'on request' (original code 2); reclassified as 'Yes - Fully Public' (3). Could not independently confirm a published rulebook specifically for the still-developing National Payment Switch/mobile-money interoperability scheme — flag that narrower point for human review.

Definition: Percentage of the adult population (15+ years) who have made at least one digital payment transaction through the instant payment system in the past 90 days, indicating active usage rather than just account ownership.
Comments: Indicators suggest a high share of adults use digital payments: BoU reports national financial inclusion at 70% and an e-payments index of 37% (FY2024/25), implying many users are active in digital financial services but not near-universal; mapped to 50–69% active users band.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Evidence conflicts and does not clearly support the original band. BoU's own FY2024/25 Integrated Annual Report cites an 'e-payments index' of 37%, which would actually fall in the 20-49% band, not 50-69%. Separately, MTN alone reports 14.7m active mobile money users against Uganda's ~27.3m adults (15+) — roughly 54% from a single operator, before adding Airtel and without clarity on overlap or the 90-day activity window used. Neither source cleanly maps to the metadata's precise definition. Flagging for human review rather than asserting a replacement code.

Definition: Whether digital payment systems and access points (apps, USSD, agents) are designed to accommodate persons with disabilities (visual, hearing, mobility, cognitive impairments), and disability-disaggregated coverage rates if data available.
Comments: Disability access efforts are present but uneven: government and financial-sector stakeholders publicly acknowledge barriers and call for stronger inclusion of persons with disabilities in financial services, with some institutions reporting initiatives to improve accessibility (suggesting partial progress rather than comprehensive nationwide accessibility standards).
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Revised down: a June 2026 Observer investigation found MTN and Airtel Uganda have made no deliberate efforts to stock accessible devices and have no published accessibility provisions (screen reader support, accessible USSD/agent protocols) for persons with disabilities, and that Uganda lacks a standalone Digital Inclusion Policy. Independent hackathon prototypes (VoicePay, EchoKash) exist but are not official, deployed operator features. The original source (a ministerial call for stronger inclusion) does not itself evidence accommodations in place. Reclassified as 'No' (Value Code 1); recommend human review given this is a fast-moving area.

Comments: Government adoption/digitization is meaningful but not near-universal: BoU notes government payments using EFTs and that ACH enhancements reduced EFT completion time “especially for government payments,” indicating substantial digitization but without evidence of >70% coverage.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: No reliable aggregate percentage of total G2P payments (salaries + pensions + social transfers) made digitally was found. Civil service payroll/pensions appear largely bank-digitised, but SAGE/DRDIP social transfers were still being piloted for full digitisation as of the Ministry of Gender's own feasibility study, and the widely-cited '93% of shillings move electronically' figure is economy-wide, not G2P-specific. Flagging for human review rather than asserting a percentage band.

Definition: Whether refugees, asylum seekers, internally displaced persons, migrants, and stateless persons can legally access and open digital payment accounts, and practical barriers or enablers for these populations.
Comments: Refugee access via digital payments is partially enabled through humanitarian mobile money transfers (e.g., agencies using Airtel/mobile money for cash transfers), but KYC/SIM registration constraints have at times limited viability and required fallback to cash, indicating partial access rather than full inclusion.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Updated with fresher (2024) evidence: refugees/asylum seekers can legally register SIM cards and mobile money using a Refugee ID or OPM attestation letter (over 600,000 with attestation letters can now access mobile services in their own name), but KYC inconsistency between MNOs/banks, digital literacy and distance to agents remain practical barriers — confirming 'Partial' (Value Code 2). The original 2017/2018 Urban Institute case study is replaced with more recent CALP/FSD Africa/UNCDF sources.
